title: Manifolds, metrics and integration
scope: Spacetime as a differentiable manifold equipped with a metric, taught intrinsically: the point-set topology and maps needed to define manifolds (open sets, continuity, homeomorphisms, Hausdorff, compactness, simple connectedness); charts, atlases, transition maps and smooth structure; smooth maps, diffeomorphisms, push-forward and pull-back; general coordinate transformations and why coordinates are labels rather than vectors; curves, tangent vectors as directional derivatives, tangent and cotangent spaces, coordinate bases, vector and tensor fields, integral curves and congruences; the metric tensor field, its components, line element, inverse, determinant, signature and operational meaning; Riemannian, Lorentzian and pseudo-Riemannian manifolds; flat metrics in disguise and standard 2D examples; local light cones read from a metric; the local flatness theorem and Riemann normal coordinates; hypersurfaces, normals, causal type, induced metrics, projection tensors, embeddings and embedding diagrams as a technique; conformally related and conformally flat metrics; tensor densities, sqrt(-g), invariant volume and hypersurface elements, and the covariant divergence theorem. Lie derivatives and isometries, connections, curvature, forms and frames, and specific spacetimes are taught elsewhere.

concepts.title: Map between sets
concepts.summary: A map f: M -> N assigns to every element of its domain exactly one element of the target set; maps compose, and the image of a subset and the inverse image of a subset of N are the basic ways of transporting sets through them.
merged_from: function versus value of a function
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur appendix C also separates the function f from its value f(x), a distinction that matters once vector fields act on functions.

concepts.title: Bijection
concepts.summary: A map is injective if distinct points go to distinct images, surjective if every target point is hit, and bijective if both; exactly the bijections have an inverse map.

concepts.title: Open set
concepts.summary: In R^n (or any metric space) a set is open if every point in it is surrounded by a small ball lying wholly inside the set; open sets formalize "all nearby points" without needing exact distances afterwards.
concepts.notes: Metric space and open balls are folded in as the setting in which open sets are first defined before abstracting to a topology.

concepts.title: Topological space
concepts.summary: A topological space is a set together with a chosen family of "open" subsets, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections and containing the empty set and the whole set; it captures nearness and continuity with no notion of distance.

concepts.title: Continuous map
concepts.summary: A map between topological spaces is continuous when the inverse image of every open set is open; equivalently, points close to x land close to f(x). This generalizes epsilon-delta continuity to spaces without distances.

concepts.title: Homeomorphism
concepts.summary: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection whose inverse is also continuous; homeomorphic spaces are topologically indistinguishable, such as a coffee mug and a doughnut, and manifolds are defined as spaces locally homeomorphic to R^n.

concepts.title: Hausdorff property
concepts.summary: A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods; the condition is imposed on manifolds to exclude pathologies such as a line with a doubled point or a branching line.

concepts.title: Compactness
concepts.summary: A set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover (for metric spaces, every sequence has a convergent subsequence inside it); by the Heine-Borel theorem the compact subsets of R^n are exactly the closed and bounded ones.
concepts.notes: Boundedness needs a distance, which is why Gifted Amateur flags it as a metric notion.

concepts.title: Simply connected space
concepts.summary: A connected space is simply connected if every closed loop can be shrunk continuously to a point, so any two paths with the same endpoints can be deformed into one another; a plane is simply connected, a plane with a hole is not.
concepts.notes: Used later for holonomy, exact forms and path independence arguments.

concepts.title: Manifold
concepts.summary: A manifold is a space in which every point has a neighbourhood that can be labelled continuously and one-to-one by n real numbers, so that small patches look like pieces of R^n while the global shape may be quite different; n is its dimension.
concepts.notes: Examples that are not manifolds: a self-crossing curve, the apex of a double cone, a line sticking out of a plane. Schutz shows the set of all rotations is a three-dimensional manifold. Standard definitions add the Hausdorff and second-countability conditions.

concepts.title: Chart
concepts.summary: A chart (U, phi) is an open region U of a manifold with a homeomorphism phi onto an open subset of R^n; the components of phi are the coordinates of each point, and functions on the manifold are handled in practice as ordinary functions of those coordinates.
concepts.notes: A function f on the manifold is represented by f composed with the inverse chart map; a map between manifolds by psi o f o phi^-1.

concepts.title: Transition map
aliases: change of coordinates on an overlap
concepts.summary: Where two charts overlap, the transition map psi o phi^-1 converts one set of coordinates of a point into the other; requiring these maps to be smooth is what lets calculus be done consistently on a manifold.

concepts.title: Atlas
concepts.summary: An atlas is a collection of charts whose domains together cover the whole manifold; many spaces, such as the sphere, need more than one chart because any single coordinate system degenerates somewhere, like polar coordinates at the origin.

names: two-chart stereographic atlas of the sphere
failure of polar coordinates at r = 0

concepts.notes: Folds in coordinate degeneracy (DIV ch05: a point where a chart fails to be one-to-one, a property of the chart not the space) and Schutz ch01 on coordinate systems that fail to cover every event. Coordinate versus curvature singularities of specific spacetimes belong to black-holes.

concepts.title: Smooth function
concepts.summary: A function on a region of R^n is of class C^k if all its partial derivatives up to order k exist and are continuous, and smooth (C-infinity) if this holds for every k.

concepts.title: Differentiable manifold
concepts.summary: A differentiable manifold is a manifold whose charts are all smoothly compatible, forming a maximal atlas, so that smoothness of functions, curves and maps does not depend on which coordinates are used; general relativity models spacetime as a four-dimensional smooth manifold.
concepts.notes: Schutz contrasts the smooth sphere with the cone, which fails at its apex. DIV ch13 notes the field equations need only a C^2 metric, with weaker conditions at matter boundaries; Gifted Amateur ch50 treats places where smoothness fails as not belonging to spacetime. "Differential geometry" mentions are folded here.

concepts.title: Local geometry versus global topology
concepts.summary: Being a manifold, or carrying a given metric, only constrains small neighbourhoods; the same local structure can be glued into different global shapes, as a flat plane, cylinder and torus share local geometry but differ in connectivity.

concepts.title: Differentiable map between manifolds
concepts.summary: A map between manifolds is differentiable (smooth) when its expression in coordinates, chart of the target composed with the map composed with inverse chart of the source, is differentiable for every choice of charts.

concepts.title: Diffeomorphism
concepts.summary: A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection between manifolds whose inverse is also smooth; diffeomorphic manifolds are the same as smooth manifolds, and in general relativity metrics related by a diffeomorphism describe the same physical spacetime.
concepts.notes: Sliding every point along the integral curves of a vector field is a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms; its generator, the Lie derivative, belongs to geodesics-and-symmetries.

concepts.title: General coordinate transformation
aliases: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation
concepts.summary: A general coordinate transformation is any smooth, locally invertible relabelling x -> x'(x); its matrix of partial derivatives dx'/dx varies from point to point and transforms tensor components at each point, and it is singular exactly where its Jacobian determinant vanishes.

names: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation

merged_from: Jacobian matrix of a coordinate transformation
concepts.notes: In curved spacetime no global Lorentz frame exists, so all such transformations must be admitted rather than only Lorentz transformations (SCH ch06). Gifted Amateur ch02 shows the Lorentz matrix is itself dx'/dx.

concepts.title: Coordinates are not vectors
aliases: position vector is not a vector
concepts.summary: Coordinates are labels for points, and the array x^mu does not transform like vector components under nonlinear coordinate changes; only infinitesimal displacements dx^mu, which live in the tangent space, transform with the Jacobian.
concepts.notes: In curved spacetime there is no arrow from one point to another, so the Cartesian position vector has no counterpart.

concepts.title: Curve on a manifold
concepts.summary: A curve is a map from an interval of a real parameter into the manifold, described in a chart by functions x^mu(lambda); the underlying set of points is the path, and reparametrizing changes the curve but not the path.

concepts.title: Tangent vector
concepts.summary: A tangent vector at a point is the velocity of a curve through it, with components dx^mu/dlambda in a chart; curves that agree to first order at the point define the same tangent vector, and such vectors live at the point rather than in the manifold.

names: tangent vector to a parametrized curve

merged_from: tangent vector to a parametrized curve
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch31 checks the definition on a straight segment, and ch30 builds the unit tangent dX/ds of curves in Euclidean space. The classical route differentiates a displacement vector X(tau) with the chain rule.

concepts.title: Tangent vector as directional derivative
aliases: vector field as directional derivative operator
concepts.summary: The modern definition identifies a tangent vector with the operator d/dlambda = (dx^mu/dlambda) partial_mu that returns the rate of change of any function along a curve; such linear, Leibniz-rule operators (derivations) correspond one-to-one with tangent vectors, and the coordinate basis vectors become the partial derivatives.

names: tangent vector as derivative along a curve
vector field as directional derivative operator

merged_from: tangent vector as derivative along a curve
vector field as directional derivative operator
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch31 writes v[f] for action on a function and v(sigma) for action on a one-form, with v[f] = <df, v>. Schutz ch06 defines the tangent as the map from the gradient of phi to d phi/d lambda.

concepts.title: Tangent space
aliases: space of vectors at a point
concepts.summary: The tangent space T_pM is the vector space of all tangent vectors at a point p, of the same dimension as the manifold; each point has its own, so vectors at different points cannot be compared or added without extra structure.

names: identification of tangent space with Minkowski space-time
why comparing vectors needs a connection

merged_from: identification of tangent space with Minkowski space-time
concepts.notes: In flat spacetime each tangent space with its metric is a copy of Minkowski space, which is why vectors and null cones can be drawn directly on the diagram there (DIV ch08); this identification fails in curved spacetime.

concepts.title: Coordinate basis
concepts.summary: A chart supplies at every point the basis e_mu = partial/partial x^mu of vectors tangent to the coordinate lines, each scaled so that moving along it by one unit advances its coordinate by one; its members commute, and their inner products are the metric components.
concepts.notes: Coordinate basis vectors are generally not unit vectors (e_theta has length r in the plane). Non-coordinate and orthonormal frames belong to differential-forms-and-frames; the Lie bracket criterion to geodesics-and-symmetries.

concepts.title: Cotangent space
aliases: space of covectors at a point
concepts.summary: The cotangent space at p is the dual of the tangent space: the linear real-valued functions on vectors at p, i.e. one-forms; the coordinate differentials dx^mu form the basis dual to partial/partial x^mu.

concepts.title: Vector field
concepts.summary: A vector field assigns a tangent vector to every point of a region, each in its own tangent space; in a chart its components are functions of the coordinates, and it acts on functions as a first-order differential operator.

concepts.title: Tensor field
concepts.summary: A tensor field assigns to each point a tensor of fixed type built from that point's tangent and cotangent spaces; its components are functions of the coordinates, and it is smooth if they are smooth in every chart.

concepts.title: Push-forward
concepts.summary: A smooth map phi from M to N carries tangent vectors forward: the push-forward of a vector at p acts on a function on N by first pulling the function back along phi, and in coordinates its components are multiplied by the Jacobian matrix of the map.
concepts.notes: DIV ch07 introduces it with a diffeomorphism taking P to Q, expressed in a single coordinate system, as groundwork for the Lie derivative (geodesics-and-symmetries). Only a diffeomorphism can push forward covariant tensors; general maps push vectors forward.

concepts.title: Pull-back
concepts.summary: A smooth map phi from M to N carries one-forms and covariant tensors backwards: the pull-back of a covariant tensor on N evaluates it on the push-forwards of vectors from M; the induced metric of a submanifold is the pull-back of the ambient metric.

concepts.title: Integral curve
aliases: integral curves of a vector field
concepts.summary: An integral curve of a vector field is a curve whose tangent at each point equals the field there, a solution of dx^mu/dlambda = V^mu(x); through each point where the field is nonzero exactly one passes locally.

names: integral curves of a vector field

merged_from: integral curves of a vector field

concepts.title: Congruence of curves
concepts.summary: A congruence is a family of curves filling a region with exactly one through each point, so the curves never cross; the integral curves of a smooth nonvanishing vector field form one, and fluid or observer world lines are physical examples.

concepts.title: Metric as additional structure
concepts.summary: A bare manifold has points, smoothness and vectors but no lengths, angles or shape; a metric is extra structure chosen on top, and different metrics on the same manifold (a round sphere and an ellipsoid) give different geometries.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch34 stacks the layers: manifold (forms, Lie derivatives), then metric (connection, curvature), then the Einstein tensor. DIV ch13 stresses that points acquire identity as events only once a metric is given.

concepts.title: Metric tensor
concepts.summary: The metric tensor is a smooth, symmetric, non-degenerate (0,2) tensor field g that gives the inner product of vectors at each point, and so fixes lengths, proper times, angles, causal character and the correspondence between vectors and one-forms; in general relativity it is the gravitational field itself.

names: metric as a symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form

concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur calls it a slot machine taking two vectors; its variation from point to point encodes gravity.

concepts.title: Metric components
concepts.summary: In a coordinate basis the metric components g_{mu nu} = g(e_mu, e_nu) form a symmetric matrix of functions of position; a metric with no off-diagonal entries is called diagonal, and position dependence of the components alone does not signal curvature.

names: degrees of freedom of a metric

merged_from: degrees of freedom of a metric
concepts.notes: An n-dimensional metric has n(n+1)/2 component functions, n of which can be changed by coordinates. Every 3-metric can be diagonalized locally (Cotton-Darboux) but a general 4-metric cannot. Cross terms carry a factor of two in the line element.

concepts.title: Line element
concepts.summary: The line element ds^2 = g_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu gives the squared interval between infinitesimally separated points; because its coefficients are the metric components, quoting it together with the coordinates specifies the metric completely.

names: coordinate transformation of a line element
what finite distance does and does not mean

merged_from: coordinate transformation of a line element
concepts.notes: Substituting new coordinates into a line element gives a different-looking expression for the same geometry; two metrics describe the same geometry if some substitution maps one onto the other (GA appD). As a tensor it is g = g_{mu nu} dx^mu (x) dx^nu.

concepts.title: Proper length of a curve
concepts.summary: The length of a curve is the integral along it of the square root of |g_{mu nu} (dx^mu/dlambda)(dx^nu/dlambda)| dlambda, independent of how the curve is parametrized; for spacelike curves it is proper length and for timelike curves the same integral gives proper time.

names: line element and interval along a curve
proper length of a spacelike curve

merged_from: line element and interval along a curve
proper length of a spacelike curve
concepts.notes: Holding all but one coordinate fixed gives the proper length element along a coordinate line, dl = sqrt(g_ii) dx^i (no sum), e.g. r dtheta in the plane (GA ch05). Extremizing this length gives geodesics (geodesics-and-symmetries).

concepts.title: Operational meaning of the metric
aliases: metric measured by rods and clocks
concepts.summary: The metric is physically measurable: a short spacelike displacement has a proper length read by a rod equal to the square root of |g(dx,dx)|, and a short timelike one has a proper time read by a clock carried between the events.

names: metric measured by rods and clocks

merged_from: metric measured by rods and clocks

concepts.title: Coordinate freedom
aliases: coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
concepts.summary: In general relativity coordinates are arbitrary labels: a coordinate called t need not measure time nor r distance, and physical durations and lengths come only from combining coordinate differences with the metric.

names: coordinates have no intrinsic metric significance
coordinates have no immediate metrical significance
coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
a metric converts labels into lengths

merged_from: coordinates have no immediate metrical significance
coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
coordinates have no intrinsic metric significance
concepts.notes: Coordinate velocity dx/dt (GA ch22) is a bookkeeping quantity, not what a local observer measures. DIV writes equations valid only in special adapted coordinates with a starred equals sign. GA uses the areal radius relabelling as an example.

concepts.title: Inverse metric
concepts.summary: The inverse metric g^{mu nu} is the symmetric (2,0) tensor whose component matrix is the inverse of g_{mu nu}, so g^{mu lambda} g_{lambda nu} = delta^mu_nu; it takes two one-forms to a number and raises indices.
concepts.notes: In a Lorentz frame eta^{mu nu} has the same numerical entries as eta_{mu nu}; in polar coordinates g^{theta theta} = 1/r^2.

concepts.title: Metric signature
concepts.summary: At any point a change of basis brings the metric matrix to diagonal form with entries +1 and -1, and the numbers of each (the signature) cannot be altered by any change of basis; spacetime has one time-like and three space-like signs, summarized as signature +2 or -2 depending on convention.

names: canonical form of the metric at a point

merged_from: canonical form of the metric at a point
concepts.notes: Schutz ch06 states the canonical form theorem (Sylvester) at a point. Gifted Amateur ch37 uses s, the number of negative eigenvalues, in sqrt((-1)^s g). The book-dependent sign choice (-+++ vs +---) is special-relativity/metric-signature-convention.

concepts.title: Riemannian metric
concepts.summary: A Riemannian metric gives every nonzero vector a positive squared length, as on ordinary surfaces; a metric that allows negative or zero squared lengths for nonzero vectors is pseudo-Riemannian.
concepts.notes: With a positive-definite metric, curve lengths between two points are bounded below, so geodesics locally minimize length (GA ch08).

concepts.title: Lorentzian metric
concepts.summary: A Lorentzian metric has one eigenvalue of one sign and the rest of the other, like Minkowski's, so every tangent space splits into timelike, null and spacelike vectors; this is the kind of metric spacetime carries.

concepts.title: Pseudo-Riemannian manifold
concepts.summary: A pseudo-Riemannian manifold is a differentiable manifold equipped with a smooth metric tensor field; with a positive-definite metric it is Riemannian, and with a Lorentzian metric it is a Lorentzian manifold.
concepts.notes: Schutz uses "Riemannian manifold" for both definite and indefinite metrics and says so explicitly.

concepts.title: Spacetime as a Lorentzian manifold
concepts.summary: General relativity models spacetime as a four-dimensional smooth manifold of events carrying a Lorentzian metric; two such pairs related by a diffeomorphism are the same physical spacetime, so a solution is really an equivalence class of metrics.
concepts.notes: Schutz ch07 splits it: Postulate I gives a manifold with a metric, Postulate III (local flatness) supplies the Lorentzian signature. Diffeomorphism invariance as a gauge symmetry of the theory is action-principles-and-field-theory.

concepts.title: Metric determinant
concepts.summary: The metric determinant g = det(g_{mu nu}) is negative for a Lorentzian metric and picks up the square of the Jacobian under coordinate changes, making it a scalar density of weight two; where it vanishes the inverse metric does not exist in that chart.
merged_from: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols
concepts.notes: For a diagonal metric it is the product of diagonal entries, e.g. g = -r^4 sin^2 theta for Minkowski in spherical coordinates. A vanishing determinant signals a coordinate or genuine singularity to be tested (GA ch26). Its derivative formula belongs to connection-and-parallel-transport.

concepts.title: Flat metric
concepts.summary: A metric is flat if some coordinate system makes its components constant with entries +1 or -1 on the diagonal throughout a region, not just at one point; the same flat metric can look complicated in other coordinates, as polar coordinates give ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2.

names: polar metric ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2

concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch26 shows a line element that looks singular but is -dT^2 + dX^2 in disguise. Checking flatness in general requires the Riemann tensor (curvature). Spatial slices can be flat while spacetime is curved (GA ch16, k = 0 cosmology).

concepts.title: Two-sphere metric
concepts.summary: A sphere of radius a has intrinsic line element ds^2 = a^2 (dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2); it is genuinely curved, and in any metric the coefficient of dOmega^2 fixes the area (4 pi times it) and circumference of the corresponding spheres.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur appD also writes it as dr^2/(1 - r^2) + r^2 dphi^2 with r the distance from the axis; Schutz ch10 uses it to define the areal radius.

concepts.title: Local light cone
concepts.summary: At each event the metric picks out the null directions with g(k,k) = 0, forming a cone that separates timelike directions (inside, available to massive bodies) from spacelike ones; in curved spacetime or curvilinear coordinates these cones tilt and narrow from place to place, and drawing them is a quick way to read a metric.

names: light cones as a picture of the metric

merged_from: light cones as a picture of the metric
concepts.notes: DIV ch19 sketches diagrams by evaluating the slope of each family of radial null rays as a function of position. Global causal structure is causal-structure-and-singularities.

concepts.title: Local flatness theorem
concepts.summary: About any point of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold one can choose coordinates in which the metric equals the Minkowski (or Euclidean) form at that point and all its first derivatives vanish there, but the second derivatives cannot all be removed; curvature lives in what remains.
concepts.notes: Schutz proves it by counting Taylor coefficients: 10 metric values vs 16 free first derivatives of the transformation, 40 first derivatives of g vs 40 second derivatives, 100 second derivatives of g vs 80 third derivatives, leaving 20 = the independent Riemann components. The 6 leftover parameters at zeroth order are the Lorentz boosts and rotations. Physical local inertial frames are equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Riemann normal coordinates
concepts.summary: Riemann normal coordinates about a point label each nearby event by the initial direction times affine distance of the geodesic reaching it from that point; they realize the local flatness theorem, with the metric Minkowskian and connection coefficients zero at the origin.
concepts.notes: The expansion of the metric to second order in these coordinates in terms of the Riemann tensor belongs to curvature.

concepts.title: Hypersurface
concepts.summary: An m-dimensional subspace of an n-dimensional manifold is given by n functions of m parameters or by n - m independent equations; a hypersurface is the case m = n - 1, a single equation f(x) = constant, such as a surface of simultaneity in spacetime.

concepts.title: Unit normal to a hypersurface
concepts.summary: The gradient of the function defining a hypersurface is a one-form that annihilates every tangent vector of the surface; raising its index with the inverse metric gives the normal vector, and dividing by its magnitude gives the unit normal, which exists only when the surface is not null.

names: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface

merged_from: unit normal to a spacelike hypersurface
concepts.notes: DIV ch14 takes the future-directed timelike unit normal of a spacelike slice. Gifted Amateur ch30 builds n from the cross product of tangent vectors of a surface in R^3, whose use for extrinsic curvature belongs to curvature.

concepts.title: Spacelike, timelike and null hypersurfaces
concepts.summary: A hypersurface is spacelike if all its tangent vectors are spacelike (its normal is timelike), timelike if it contains timelike directions (spacelike normal), and null if its normal is null and lies within it; the sign of g^{mu mu} likewise classifies the level surfaces of a coordinate x^mu.
concepts.notes: Schutz ch03 labels surfaces by the type of their normal, the opposite of standard usage, a known source of confusion. DIV ch17 uses g^{rr} and g^{tt} to decide whether r or t is a timelike coordinate. Foliations and evolution of slices belong to einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Induced metric
concepts.summary: A submanifold inherits a metric from its surroundings by restricting the ambient metric to its tangent vectors; in practice one substitutes the embedding functions into the ambient line element, g_{mu nu} = G_{alpha beta} (dX^alpha/dx^mu)(dX^beta/dx^nu).

names: induced metric in a pseudo-Euclidean ambient space

merged_from: induced metric in a pseudo-Euclidean ambient space
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur appD gives two methods: parametric substitution (method I) and differentiating an implicit equation (method II), with worked examples: circle a^2 dtheta^2, paraboloid (1 + a^2 r^2) dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2, torus (c + a cos v)^2 du^2 + a^2 dv^2, and the one-sheet hyperboloid in (2+1) Minkowski space whose induced metric is Lorentzian (2D de Sitter). In an indefinite ambient space the induced metric can be Riemannian, Lorentzian or degenerate. DIV ch14 writes h_ab = g_ab - n_a n_b and flips its sign to a positive-definite gamma_ab.

concepts.title: Hypersurface projection tensor
concepts.summary: Given a unit normal n, the mixed tensor delta^a_b - n^a n_b (with the sign set by whether n is timelike or spacelike) removes the normal part of any vector or covector, leaving its component tangent to the hypersurface; lowering its index gives the induced metric.
concepts.notes: The analogous projector orthogonal to a four-velocity is in matter-and-stress-energy.

concepts.title: Embedding
concepts.summary: An isometric embedding places a space inside a higher-dimensional flat space by a smooth one-to-one map whose induced metric reproduces the space's own distances; it is a visual aid only, since general relativity describes spacetime intrinsically with no surrounding space.
concepts.notes: Nash showed every Riemannian manifold embeds isometrically in some Euclidean space of high enough dimension; sometimes only a patch can be embedded in R^3, e.g. part of d chi^2 + cosh^2 chi d phi^2 (GA appD).

concepts.title: Embedding diagram
concepts.summary: An embedding diagram draws a two-dimensional slice of a curved space as a surface in flat three-dimensional space whose intrinsic distances match the slice's metric; only distances measured along the surface mean anything, and the extra direction is fictitious.
concepts.notes: For a slice g_uu du^2 + R(u)^2 dphi^2, trying a surface of revolution reduces the task to (dR/du)^2 + (dZ/du)^2 = g_uu, solvable only where g_uu >= (dR/du)^2. Specific diagrams (Flamm paraboloid, wormhole throats, cosmological slices) belong with their spacetimes.

concepts.title: Conformally related metrics
concepts.summary: Two metrics on the same manifold are conformally related if one is a positive function Omega^2 times the other at every point; the rescaling changes lengths and curvature but preserves angles, ratios of lengths at a point and the light cones.
concepts.notes: Conformal compactification chooses Omega to vanish at infinity (causal-structure-and-singularities). DIV ch14 writes the spatial metric as psi^4 times a background to turn the Hamiltonian constraint into an elliptic equation (einstein-field-equations).

concepts.title: Conformal invariance
concepts.summary: A quantity is conformally invariant if it is unchanged when the metric is replaced by a conformally related one; angles, null cones, null geodesics as paths, and the Weyl tensor with one index raised are invariant, while lengths, Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor are not.

names: conformal invariance of the light-cone structure

merged_from: conformal invariance of the light-cone structure

concepts.title: Conformally flat metric
concepts.summary: A metric is conformally flat if some coordinates write it as a positive function times a flat metric; every two-dimensional metric is locally conformally flat, which for Lorentzian 2-spaces means choosing the null curves as coordinate lines, ds^2 = F^2 (dt^2 - dx^2).
concepts.notes: The test for conformal flatness in four dimensions (vanishing Weyl tensor) belongs to curvature. DIV ch24 writes the constant-curvature 3-metric in this form.

concepts.title: Hyperbolic plane
concepts.summary: The hyperbolic plane is the two-dimensional space of constant negative curvature; the half-plane model ds^2 = (dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2 and the Poincare disc map it into finite regions while preserving angles, with geodesics drawn as circular arcs meeting the boundary at right angles.

names: geodesics of the Poincare half plane
boundary at infinity of the Poincare half plane
non-embeddability of the hyperbolic plane in R^3

merged_from: geodesics of the Poincare half plane
boundary at infinity of the Poincare half plane
non-embeddability of the hyperbolic plane in R^3
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch09 computes its connection coefficients; ch16 uses the disc for k = -1 space; ch19 uses it to motivate conformal compactification (Escher-style tilings).

concepts.title: Tensor density
concepts.summary: A tensor density of weight W transforms like an ordinary tensor with the same indices except for an extra factor of the Jacobian determinant to the power W; products add weights, and multiplying by sqrt(-g) raises the weight by one.
concepts.notes: DIV writes weight +1 densities in gothic type, e.g. gothic g^ab = sqrt(-g) g^ab, and Gifted Amateur ch40 holds the densitized current sqrt(-g) J^a fixed when varying the metric. Sign conventions for W differ with the direction of the Jacobian.

concepts.title: Square root of minus the metric determinant
concepts.summary: On a Lorentzian manifold g < 0, and sqrt(-g) is a positive scalar density of weight one; it is the factor that converts coordinate volumes into proper volumes and ordinary tensors into densities.

names: square root of minus the metric determinant

merged_from: square root of minus the metric determinant
concepts.notes: For a positive-definite metric one uses sqrt(g); in general sqrt(|g|), written sqrt((-1)^s g) by Gifted Amateur.

concepts.title: Invariant volume element
concepts.summary: The coordinate cell d^4x is not invariant (it is a density of weight -1), but sqrt(-g) d^4x is: it gives the physically measured four-volume of a small cell in any coordinates, and integrating a scalar against it yields a coordinate-independent result.

names: metric determinant factor in the volume form
volume element as a scalar density of weight -1
additivity of scalars at different points
sqrt(-g) d^4x from the transformation law

merged_from: metric determinant factor in the volume form
volume element as a scalar density of weight -1

concepts.notes: For a diagonal metric areas and volumes follow from square roots of diagonal entries, e.g. r^2 sin theta dtheta dphi on a sphere and sqrt(g_11 g_22 g_33) d^3x. An observer with four-velocity u measures spatial volume sqrt(-g) u^0 d^3x (GA ch37). The volume-form viewpoint belongs to differential-forms-and-frames. It makes the action and delta^(4)/sqrt(-g) scalars.

concepts.title: Hypersurface element
concepts.summary: A small piece of a three-dimensional hypersurface is represented by a covector along its normal whose size is its three-volume, dS_mu; the flux of a current J through it is J^mu dS_mu, and integrating gives the total charge crossing the surface.

concepts.title: Covariant divergence theorem
concepts.summary: The integral of the covariant divergence of a vector field over a spacetime region, taken with sqrt(-g) d^4x, equals the flux of the field through the region's boundary; it works because sqrt(-g) V^mu_;mu = (sqrt(-g) V^mu)_,mu, and for a conserved current it says what enters a region must leave.
